extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers in humor studies, folklore, anthropology, and conference presenters for SIEF2021
extracted.subtask_description: Call/panel description and accepted-paper abstracts inviting scholarly work on the ambivalent, awkward, and transgressive aspects of humor and comedy, including both verbal and visual forms and their production/consumption. Targets empirical, theoretical, and methodological contributions for a conference panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on ambivalent, awkward, and transgressive aspects of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: This panel explores the ambivalent, awkward, and transgressive aspects of humor and comedy as employed to mark, cross, reinforce, and transgress social and cultural norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers should engage with humor's ambivalence (its ability to produce and dispel anxiety), awkwardness as a trope, and ways comedy transgresses norms. The long abstract frames humor as 'a pleasure spectacle of form's self-violation' and encourages attention to effects that 'leak over every conceivable border.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss both verbal and visual forms of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: We welcome papers that discuss both verbal and visual forms of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions may analyze jokes, narratives, stand-up, memes, images, and other visual media — any modality of humor is in scope. Comparative work across modalities is explicitly encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address production and consumption of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: We welcome papers that discuss ... the production and consumption of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions may examine creators (performers, authors, meme-makers), audiences, and the social/practical contexts in which humor is produced, circulated, and received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze how humor marks, crosses, reinforces, and transgresses social and cultural norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in humor and comedy as the simultaneous marking, crossing, reinforcing, and transgressing of social and cultural norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers should attend to the normative work of humor — how it signals boundaries, challenges or upholds hierarchies, and participates in social regulation or resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine stand-up comedy as transgressive personal disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider stand-up comedy as personal disclosure on a public arena that often purposefully breaks the quotidian social contract of what comprises civil talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses may focus on the staged role of the comedian, performance context, audience relations, and how personal disclosure functions as rule-breaking; both onstage and offstage contexts (e.g., press, social media) are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use awkwardness as a comedy trope that bends/suspends social rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Awkwardness as a comedy trope that bends and suspends all rules of social conduct for maximally (un)pleasant affective response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work can analyze awkwardness as an aesthetic/affective strategy, how it produces humor, and its social consequences or limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study upending of audience expectations and genre boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in simply an upending of the audience's expectations of genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers can investigate genre-mixing, boundary-crossing performances, or moments when expected genre conventions are deliberately violated to produce comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the political potential and risks of satire and political humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention to the increasingly effacing boundaries between political discourse and (political) satire and the 'unprecedented political potential of humor' in contemporary contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions may evaluate humor's political functions, unintended consequences, and potential dangers when satire enters political discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze defensive postures of comedians over offensive material
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore how stand-up comedians defend offensive material by reaffirming the 'role' of the comedian as inveterate truthteller, permitted to leave no topic unexplored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate rhetoric and strategies used by comedians and their communities to justify transgressive material, including on- and offstage discourse and responses from critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame and interrogate 'going too far' in comedy and taboo literatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the issue of 'going too far' within both vernacular and academic literatures on comedy and taboo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should situate debates about offensiveness and limits within broader cultural conversations and scholarship on taboo, exploring criteria and contests over boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize humorous/traumatic narratives within local and collective memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextualize particular humorous anecdotes (even those about sexual violence) within wider local narratives of war, sexual violence, and collective self-image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnographic sensitivity is required: attention to depersonalization, narrative positioning (who is named/unnamed), and how humor functions within collective trauma and memory narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply intersectional perspectives to how comedy challenges/recreates norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply an intersectional perspective to analyze how stand-up comedians and audiences both challenge and recreate cultural notions and norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should consider multiple intersecting power structures (gender, race, class, etc.), how they are reinforced or undermined by humor, and how performers' backgrounds shape material and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ empirical methods: observations, interviews, focus groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical approaches such as observations at comedy clubs, interviews with comedians, and focus groups with audience members are recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological transparency about field sites, sampling, and analytic approach is expected; mixed qualitative methods that center performer and audience perspectives are encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study humour in times of calamity: moral negotiation and civil discourse shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how 'disaster humour' breaks and bends civil discourse, its uses and abuses in negotiating morality and making sense of unprecedented experiences (e.g., COVID-19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers may analyze memes, workplace jokes, gallows humor, and social media expressions to understand collective coping, moral debates, and discursive shifts during crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address challenges and innovations in researching online humour during crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss challenges and possible innovations in collecting and researching online expressions of humour in times of calamity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions should reflect on methodological and ethical issues of online data collection, curation, representation, and interpretation, and propose novel solutions or tools.
